title: Aeson
titleEn: The Renewal of Aeson — Metamorphoses VII.159–296
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin.
about: Jason is back from Colchis and Thessaly is giving thanks for the sons it has returned to it, but his father Aeson is too near death to stand among the grateful. Jason asks Medea to take years off his own life and add them to his father; she refuses that exchange and promises a greater gift out of her own art. At the full moon she leaves the house alone at midnight, calls on Night, on Hecate, on Earth and on the powers of wood and water, and rides a chariot drawn by winged dragons for nine days and nine nights, gathering herbs. What she boils out of them she pours into the old man's opened throat once the old blood has run out, and the part closes with Bacchus, who has watched from above, taking the same gift for his own nurses.

sentences.t:
Haemoniae matres pro gnatis dona receptis
grandaevique ferunt patres congestaque flamma
tura liquefaciunt, inductaque cornibus aurum
victima vota cadit.
sentences.l: The Haemonian mothers, for their sons received back, bring gifts, and the aged fathers do, and on the heaped-up flame they melt frankincense, and, having had gold drawn over its horns, the vowed victim falls.
sentences.i: The mothers of Haemonia bring offerings for the sons they have back, and the aged fathers with them; they melt frankincense on the piled fire, and the promised victim, its horns gilded, falls.
sentences.n: Haemonia is Thessaly, and the sons received back are the Argonauts, home from Colchis. inducta cornibus aurum: inducta is a passive participle used in the middle sense and keeping an accusative of its own, aurum — “having had gold drawn over its horns”, that is, the beast is gilded for sacrifice. victima vota is the animal already promised to a god in a vow, so the offering discharges a debt.

sentences.t:
Sed abest gratantibus Aeson,
iam propior leto fessusque senilibus annis.
sentences.l: But Aeson is absent from those giving thanks, already nearer to death and worn out by the years of an old man.
sentences.i: But Aeson is missing from the rejoicing, already nearer to death, worn out with an old man's years.
sentences.n: Aeson is Jason's father. gratantibus is a dative with abest, “he is away from those giving thanks”, and propior likewise governs the dative leto, “nearer to death”. The line sets one absence against the whole town's celebration.

sentences.t:
Cum sic Aesonides: “O cui debere salutem
confiteor, coniunx, quamquam mihi cuncta dedisti
excessitque fidem meritorum summa tuorum,
sentences.l: When thus the son of Aeson: “O you to whom I confess that I owe my safety, wife — although you have given me everything, and the sum of your services has gone beyond belief —
sentences.i: Then the son of Aeson spoke: “You to whom I confess I owe my life, my wife — though you have given me everything, and the sum of what you have done for me passes belief —
sentences.n: Cum sic Aesonides: the verb of speaking is simply left out, “thus [spoke] the son of Aeson”, a compression Latin allows and English does not. Aesonides is a patronymic, “son of Aeson” — Jason. excessit fidem, “has gone beyond credence”, means the total is past believing, not past repaying.

sentences.t:
si tamen hoc possunt (quid enim non carmina possunt?),
deme meis annis et demptos adde parenti.”
sentences.l: if however they can do this (for what can spells not do?), take away from my years and add the ones taken away to my father.”
sentences.i: if even so they can do this — for what can spells not do? — take from my years, and add what you take to my father.”
sentences.n: carmina here are incantations, not poems; the plural subject of the first possunt is named only inside the parenthesis. deme takes the dative meis annis, “take from my years”, matching adde parenti, “add to my father”, in the same line; demptos is the participle standing as its own noun, “the ones taken away”. Jason asks for a transfer, not a cure — which is exactly the word Medea will pick up on next.

sentences.t:
Nec tenuit lacrimas. Mota est pietate rogantis,
dissimilemque animum subiit Aeeta relictus.
sentences.l: Nor did he hold back his tears. She was moved by the devotion of the one asking, and Aeetes, left behind, came up into her unlike mind.
sentences.i: He could not hold back his tears. She was moved by the asking man's love for his father, and Aeetes, abandoned, rose into her mind — a mind so unlike his.
sentences.n: pietas is the duty and love owed to a parent; Jason's for Aeson is what moves her. subiit takes the accusative animum, “came up into her mind”, and dissimilem marks the comparison she makes silently: Medea deserted her own father Aeetes when she fled Colchis. Aeeta is the Greek nominative form of the name.

sentences.t:
Nec tamen adfectus tales confessa “quod” inquit
“excidit ore tuo, coniunx, scelus? ergo ego cuiquam
posse tuae videor spatium transcribere vitae?
sentences.l: Yet not having confessed such feelings, she says: “What crime has fallen out of your mouth, husband? So do I seem able to sign over to anyone the span of your life?
sentences.i: But she confessed no such feeling. “What crime,” she said, “has escaped your lips, husband? So I seem able to make over the span of your life to somebody else?
sentences.n: confessa is the perfect participle of the deponent confiteor and is active in sense: “not having confessed such feelings”, that is, she keeps the thought of her father to herself. excidit ore tuo, “has fallen out of your mouth”, is the idiom for a word let slip. transcribere belongs to the ledger — it is the verb for signing property over to another name — and it is Medea's word for what Jason has just asked.

sentences.t:
Nec sinat hoc Hecate, nec tu petis aequa. Sed isto,
quod petis, experiar maius dare munus Iason.
sentences.l: Nor may Hecate allow this, nor do you ask for fair things. But I shall try to give a greater gift than that which you ask, Jason.
sentences.i: May Hecate not permit it — and what you ask is not just. But I will try to give you a greater gift than the one you ask for, Jason.
sentences.n: sinat is an optative subjunctive, “may she not allow”. isto, quod petis is an ablative of comparison with maius, “greater than that which you ask”. aequa is neuter plural, “fair things”: she refuses on principle, not out of unwillingness. Hecate is the goddess of witchcraft, and Medea is her priestess.

sentences.t:
Arte mea soceri longum temptabimus aevum,
non annis renovare tuis: modo diva triformis
adiuvet et praesens ingentibus adnuat ausis.”
sentences.l: By my art we shall attempt to renew the long lifetime of your father, not by your years: only let the three-formed goddess help, and, present, nod assent to our huge daring.”
sentences.i: By my own art we will attempt to renew your father's long span of years, not with your own: only let the three-formed goddess help, and be present, and nod her assent to so great a daring.”
sentences.n: socer is a father-in-law: Aeson is Medea's. Magnus prints renovare, “to renew”; some editions print revocare, “to call back”. modo with the subjunctive adiuvet is a proviso, “only let her help”. The three-formed goddess is Hecate again, worshipped in three shapes; praesens of a god means present and working, not merely nearby, and adnuat governs the dative ausis, “nod assent to the daring deeds”.

sentences.t:
Tres aberant noctes, ut cornua tota coirent
efficerentque orbem.
sentences.l: Three nights were wanting, for the horns to come wholly together and make a full circle.
sentences.i: Three nights were still to pass before the horns of the moon would meet completely and make a full circle.
sentences.n: The horns are the tips of the crescent moon, which close at the full. ut with the subjunctive here states what the three nights are still wanting for, “three nights were lacking for the horns to close”.

sentences.t:
Postquam plenissima fulsit
et solida terras spectavit imagine luna,
sentences.l: After the moon shone at its fullest and looked upon the lands with an unbroken shape,
sentences.i: When the moon had shone at her fullest and looked down on the earth with her disc entire,
sentences.n: solida imagine is an ablative of manner, “with an unbroken shape” — the whole disc, no longer horned. luna is the subject of both fulsit and spectavit and is held back to the very end of its clause, so the sentence only resolves on the last word.

sentences.t:
egreditur tectis vestes induta recinctas,
nuda pedem, nudos umeris infusa capillos,
fertque vagos mediae per muta silentia noctis
incomitata gradus.
sentences.l: she goes out from the house, having put on ungirt robes, bare as to her foot, having her bare hair poured over her shoulders, and unaccompanied she carries her wandering steps through the mute silences of the middle of the night.
sentences.i: she comes out of the house in robes let loose, one foot bare, her unbound hair spilling over her shoulders, and carries her wandering steps alone through the mute silence of midnight.
sentences.n: Three Greek-looking constructions in two lines. induta vestes recinctas and infusa capillos are passive participles used in the middle sense, each keeping an accusative — “having put on ungirt robes”, “having her hair poured down”. nuda pedem is the Greek accusative of respect, “bare in respect of the foot”: the accusative names the part affected, a borrowing from Greek that only verse allows. Loose robe, bare foot, unbound hair: nothing about her is tied or knotted.

sentences.t:
Homines volucresque ferasque
solverat alta quies: nullo cum murmure saepes,
inmotaeque silent frondes, silet umidus aer;
sidera sola micant.
sentences.l: Deep rest had loosened men and birds and beasts: with no murmur the hedges, and the unmoved leaves, are silent; the damp air is silent; the stars alone glitter.
sentences.i: Deep sleep had unstrung men and birds and beasts alike: hedge and unstirring leaf are silent, not a murmur in them; the damp air is silent; only the stars glitter.
sentences.n: solverat, “had loosened”: sleep undoes the limbs, as if untying them. saepes has no verb of its own and borrows silent from the following line. The chain of -que endings piles the three kinds of living creature up without pause, and then the three silences answer them.

sentences.t:
Ad quae sua bracchia tendens
ter se convertit, ter sumptis flumine crinem
inroravit aquis ternisque ululatibus ora
solvit et, in dura submisso poplite terra,
sentences.l: And stretching her arms toward them, three times she turned herself around, three times she bedewed her hair with waters taken from the river, and with three howls she loosed her mouth, and, with her knee lowered onto the hard ground,
sentences.i: Stretching her arms toward them, she turned herself about three times, three times sprinkled her hair with water taken from the river, and opened her lips in three long cries; then, with her knee down on the hard ground,
sentences.n: Ad quae is a connecting relative, “and toward them” — toward the stars just named; Latin opens a new sentence with a relative where English starts again with “and”. Everything comes in threes here, ter, ter, ternis, for the three-formed goddess. crinem is the plain accusative object of inroravit and aquis the ablative of the liquid, “she bedewed her hair with water”. in dura submisso poplite terra is a true ablative absolute, “with her knee lowered onto the hard earth”, a construction with no grammatical tie to the rest of the sentence.

sentences.t:
“Nox” ait “arcanis fidissima, quaeque diurnis
aurea cum luna succeditis ignibus astra,
sentences.l: “Night,” she says, “most faithful to secret things, and you stars who with the golden moon come after the fires of day,
sentences.i: “Night,” she said, “most faithful of all to secrets, and you stars who follow in after the fires of day, with the golden moon,
sentences.n: arcanis is a dative with fidissima, “most faithful to secret things”. In quaeque ... astra the verb is second person plural, succeditis, because she is speaking to the stars, and succedo takes the dative ignibus, “come after the fires”. The invocation she begins here does not reach its own verb until adeste, at the close of the roll-call of powers.

sentences.t:
tuque triceps Hecate, quae coeptis conscia nostris
adiutrixque venis cantusque artisque magorum,
quaeque magos, Tellus, pollentibus instruis herbis,
sentences.l: and you three-headed Hecate, who come as one privy to our undertakings and as helper of the incantation and the art of the magicians, and you, Earth, who equip the magicians with potent herbs,
sentences.i: and you, three-headed Hecate, who come sharing in what we begin and helping the chant and the craft of the mages, and you, Earth, who arm the mages with herbs of power,
sentences.n: triceps Hecate, “three-headed”, is the same goddess as the diva triformis above. conscia takes the dative coeptis nostris, “privy to our undertakings”, and adiutrix the genitive cantus artisque, “helper of the incantation and the art”; both stand as predicates to venis, “you come as ...”. magi are eastern sorcerers, a borrowed word for a borrowed craft. instruis takes an accusative of the person and an ablative of what he is furnished with.

sentences.t:
auraeque et venti montesque amnesque lacusque
dique omnes nemorum, dique omnes noctis adeste.
sentences.l: and breezes and winds and mountains and rivers and lakes, and all you gods of the groves, and all you gods of night, be present.
sentences.i: breezes and winds, mountains and rivers and lakes, all you gods of the woodlands and all you gods of night — be here.
sentences.n: adeste, the plural imperative, is the verb the whole invocation has been waiting for since Nox. The unbroken chain of -que endings keeps the list sounding unfinished, which is how a summons works: it names until nothing is left out.

sentences.t:
Quorum ope, cum volui, ripis mirantibus amnes
in fontes rediere suos, concussaque sisto,
stantia concutio cantu freta,
sentences.l: By whose help, when I have wished it, with the banks marvelling, rivers have gone back into their own springs, and I still the shaken seas, I shake the standing seas with my chant,
sentences.i: By their help, whenever I have willed it, rivers have run back into their own springs while the banks looked on in wonder; I still the sea when it is shaken and shake it when it stands still, with my chant;
sentences.n: Quorum is a connecting relative, “and by their help”. rediere is the poetic third-person plural perfect for redierunt — this shortened -ere ending turns up regularly in verse, and it recurs several times below. ripis mirantibus is an ablative absolute, “with the banks marvelling”. One noun, freta, carries both participles and both verbs cross over it: she stills what is moving and moves what is still.

sentences.t:
nubila pello
nubilaque induco, ventos abigoque vocoque,
vipereas rumpo verbis et carmine fauces,
sentences.l: I drive the clouds away and I bring the clouds on, I both drive off the winds and call them, I burst snaky jaws with words and with chanting,
sentences.i: I drive the clouds off and I bring the clouds on; I banish the winds and call them back; with words and chanting I burst the throats of snakes;
sentences.n: The paired -que ... -que in abigoque vocoque puts the two opposite powers on one footing, “both drive off and call”. vipereas fauces is an adjective doing a genitive's work, “snaky jaws” for “the jaws of snakes”. rumpo of a snake's throat means bursting it apart by the spell alone, with no hand laid on it.

sentences.t:
vivaque saxa sua convulsaque robora terra
et silvas moveo, iubeoque tremescere montes
et mugire solum manesque exire sepulcris.
sentences.l: and living rocks, and oaks torn out of their own ground, and forests I move, and I order the mountains to tremble and the ground to bellow and the shades of the dead to come out of their tombs.
sentences.i: I move living rock, and oaks wrenched out of their own soil, and whole forests; I order the mountains to shudder, the ground to bellow, and the dead to come out of their tombs.
sentences.n: viva saxa are rocks still rooted in the earth, not quarried stone. sua terra is an ablative of separation with convulsa, “torn out of their own ground”. iubeo takes three infinitives, tremescere, mugire, exire, each with its own accusative subject. manes are the spirits of the dead; sepulcris is again ablative of separation, “out of their tombs”.

sentences.t:
Te quoque, Luna, traho, quamvis Temesaea labores
aera tuos minuant; currus quoque carmine nostro
pallet avi, pallet nostris Aurora venenis.
sentences.l: You too, Moon, I draw down, although Temesaean bronzes lessen your labors; my grandfather's chariot too grows pale at our chant, Aurora grows pale at our poisons.
sentences.i: You too, Moon, I drag down, though the bronze of Temese relieves your struggles; my grandfather's chariot goes pale at my chant, and the Dawn goes pale at my poisons.
sentences.n: Witches were said to draw the moon down out of the sky; her labores are the eclipse, and bronze from Temese, a town famous for its copper, was beaten to help her through it. The grandfather is the Sun: Medea's father Aeetes is his son, so the chariot that pales is the Sun's own. Watch quoque here and in the next lines — it is the adverb “also”, not the ablative quo with -que attached, which would mean “and by which”.

sentences.t:
Vos mihi taurorum flammas hebetastis et unco
impatiens oneris collum pressistis aratro,
sentences.l: You for me blunted the flames of the bulls, and with the hooked plough you pressed down the neck that would not endure the load,
sentences.i: You for me dulled the fire of the bulls, and forced under the hooked plough a neck that would take no burden,
sentences.n: The bulls are the fire-breathing bulls of Aeetes that Jason had to yoke to win the fleece. hebetastis is the syncopated perfect for hebetavistis, a contraction verse likes. mihi is a dative of advantage, “for me”, and impatiens takes the genitive oneris, “not enduring the load”.

sentences.t:
vos serpentigenis in se fera bella dedistis
custodemque rudem somno sopistis et aurum
vindice decepto Graias misistis in urbes.
sentences.l: you gave to the serpent-born savage wars against themselves, and you put the guardian, a novice at it, to sleep with sleep, and, the defender deceived, you sent the gold into Greek cities.
sentences.i: you set the serpent-born at savage war with one another; you drowned in sleep the guardian who had never known it; and, its defender tricked, you sent the gold away into the cities of Greece.
sentences.n: The serpent-born are the armed men who sprang from the dragon's teeth Jason sowed, and in se, “against themselves”, is how they destroyed one another. The guardian is the sleepless dragon of the fleece: Magnus prints somno, the ablative of means, “you lulled him with sleep”, leaving rudem absolute, “a novice at it”; some editions print somni, which makes it a genitive, “unacquainted with sleep”. vindice decepto is an ablative absolute. The gold is the golden fleece.

sentences.t:
Nunc opus est sucis, per quos renovata senectus
in florem redeat primosque reconligat annos.
sentences.l: Now there is need of juices, through which old age, made new, may return into flower and gather up again its first years.
sentences.i: Now what is needed are the juices by which old age, made new, may come back into flower and gather up its earliest years again.
sentences.n: opus est takes the ablative sucis, “there is need of juices”. redeat and reconligat are subjunctives in a relative clause of purpose, “juices by which it may return”. reconligat is the edition's older spelling of recolligat, with the prefix not yet assimilated to the l; Lectorium prints its witness as it stands. in florem treats a man's age as a plant's season.

sentences.t:
Et dabitis. Neque enim micuerunt sidera frustra,
nec frustra volucrum tractus cervice draconum
currus adest.”
sentences.l: And you will give them. For the stars have not glittered in vain, nor in vain is the chariot here, drawn by the neck of winged dragons.”
sentences.i: And you will give them. For the stars have not glittered for nothing, and it is not for nothing that the chariot is here, drawn by the necks of winged dragons.”
sentences.n: dabitis is a flat future used as a command, “and you will give them” — she does not ask the gods twice. tractus cervice is the ablative of the means by which the chariot is drawn, and volucrum ... draconum wraps around the whole phrase in an interlocked order that puts the dragons at both ends.

sentences.t: Aderat demissus ab aethere currus.
sentences.l: The chariot was there, sent down from the upper air.
sentences.i: The chariot was there, let down out of the sky.
sentences.n: The single line answers her own adest with aderat: she says the chariot is here, and it was. aether is the bright upper sky, distinct from the umidus aer, the damp lower air, of the night around her.

sentences.t:
Quo simul adscendit frenataque colla draconum
permulsit manibusque leves agitavit habenas,
sublimis rapitur subiectaque Thessala Tempe
despicit et Threces regionibus applicat angues:
sentences.l: Onto which as soon as she had climbed, and had stroked the bridled necks of the dragons, and with her hands had shaken the light reins, she is snatched away on high, and looks down on Thessalian Tempe set beneath her, and brings her snakes to Thracian regions:
sentences.i: As soon as she had climbed aboard, stroked the bridled necks of the dragons and shaken the light reins in her hands, she is snatched up on high; she looks down on Thessalian Tempe lying beneath her, and brings her serpents to Thracian country:
sentences.n: Quo is a connecting relative, “and onto it”. sublimis is a nominative adjective doing an adverb's work, “she is carried off, high up”. Tempe is the Thessalian valley of the Peneus, a Greek neuter plural that does not decline. On Threces: the word as printed is the plural of the noun Threx, “a Thracian”, and it will not construe here — it cannot agree with the dative regionibus, and taken as an accusative beside angues it would make the snakes themselves Thracians; the rendering above takes it in the only sense the word carries, “Thracian”. Some editions print certis, “to certain regions”, which is what the sense wants, since the mountains she surveys next are all Thessalian. Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t:
et quasque Ossa tulit quasque altus Pelion herbas
Othrysque Pindusque et Pindo maior Olympus
perspicit, et placitas partim radice revellit,
partim succidit curvamine falcis aenae.
sentences.l: and the herbs which Ossa bore, and which lofty Pelion and Othrys and Pindus and Olympus greater than Pindus bore, she looks over, and the ones that have pleased her she partly tears up by the root, partly cuts down with the curve of a bronze sickle.
sentences.i: and she scans the herbs that Ossa bore, and lofty Pelion, and Othrys and Pindus, and Olympus that is higher than Pindus; the ones she approves she tears up by the root, or else cuts with the curve of a bronze sickle.
sentences.n: All five are Thessalian mountains or on its borders; tulit, “bore”, is used of ground bringing a plant forth. Pindo maior is an ablative of comparison, “greater than Pindus”. placitas is the perfect participle of placeo standing as the object, “the ones having pleased her”. partim ... partim divides the harvest into two methods, and the sickle is bronze, the older metal kept for cutting of this kind.

sentences.t:
Multa quoque Apidani placuerunt gramina ripis,
multa quoque Amphrysi neque eras inmunis, Enipeu;
nec non Peneos, nec non Spercheides undae
contribuere aliquid iuncosaque litora Boebes.
sentences.l: Many grasses on the banks of the Apidanus also pleased her, many also on those of the Amphrysus, and you were not exempt, Enipeus; the Peneos too, and the Spercheian waters, contributed something, and the rushy shores of Boebe.
sentences.i: Many plants on the banks of the Apidanus pleased her too, and many on the Amphrysus; nor did you go untaxed, Enipeus; the Peneos gave its share, and the waters of Spercheus, and the reedy shore of Lake Boebe.
sentences.n: All of these are Thessalian waters. Ovid breaks off the account to speak to one of them directly — neque eras inmunis, Enipeu, “nor were you exempt” — turning aside to address a river as though it were standing there; the vocative Enipeu keeps its Greek ending. inmunis is the word for a man let off a public levy, so the river is being taxed like a district. nec non, a double negative, is a strong affirmative, “and also”. contribuere is again the poetic perfect for contribuerunt.

sentences.t:
Carpsit et Euboica vivax Anthedone gramen,
nondum mutato vulgatum corpore Glauci.
sentences.l: She plucked too, at Euboean Anthedon, the long-lived grass, not yet made common knowledge, the body of Glaucus not yet changed.
sentences.i: She gathered too, at Anthedon in Euboea, the grass that gives long life — not yet famous, since the body of Glaucus had not yet been transformed.
sentences.n: nondum mutato corpore Glauci is an ablative absolute, “with the body of Glaucus not yet changed”, while vulgatum, “made common knowledge”, agrees with gramen, and nondum carries over to it from the ablative absolute. Glaucus was a fisherman of Anthedon who tasted a herb there and became a sea-god; at the moment Medea passes, that has not yet happened, so the plant is still unknown to anyone but her. vivax, “long-lived”, names in the plant the long life it gives; the same word returns of the stag below.

sentences.t:
Et iam nona dies curru pennisque draconum
nonaque nox omnes lustrantem viderat agros,
cum rediit.
sentences.l: And now the ninth day and the ninth night had seen her ranging over all the fields with the chariot and the wings of the dragons, when she returned.
sentences.i: By now the ninth day and the ninth night had watched her range over every field with her chariot and the dragons' wings, when she came back.
sentences.n: dies is feminine here, nona dies, as it is when it means one particular day. lustrantem, “her ranging over”, is the accusative participle serving as the object of viderat with no pronoun expressed at all. Nine days and nine nights: the number is ritual, like the threes at the start of the invocation.

sentences.t:
Neque erant tacti, nisi odore, dracones,
et tamen annosae pellem posuere senectae.
sentences.l: And the dragons had not been touched, except by the smell, and nevertheless they laid aside the skin of their many-yeared old age.
sentences.i: The dragons had not been touched by anything but the scent, and even so they shed the skin of their long old age.
sentences.n: odore is the ablative of the means of touching, “touched by nothing except the smell” — the herbs work at a distance, on creatures not meant to be treated at all. posuere is once more the poetic perfect for posuerunt. Latin uses pono of a snake laying its skin aside, and the sloughing is the first sign the gathering has worked; annosae senectae, “of aged old age”, doubles the idea deliberately.

sentences.t:
Constitit adveniens citra limenque foresque
et tantum caelo tegitur refugitque viriles
contactus statuitque aras de caespite binas,
dexteriore Hecates, ast laeva parte Iuventae.
sentences.l: Arriving, she halted on the near side of both threshold and doors, and is covered by the sky alone, and shrank back from male contacts, and set up two altars of turf, Hecate's on the righthand side, but Youth's on the left.
sentences.i: She came and stopped short of the threshold and the doors, roofed by the sky alone; she kept clear of any man's touch and raised two altars of cut turf — Hecate's on the right, Youth's on the left.
sentences.n: citra, “on the near side of”, keeps her outside the house: she stops before threshold and door rather than entering, and the doubled limenque foresque is the elevated manner of naming a thing twice. Ovid slips into the present with tegitur, “she is covered”, between two perfects. Iuventa is the goddess Youth, the altar that names what the whole rite is for; Hecate, goddess of night and witchcraft, takes the right.

sentences.t:
Has ubi verbenis silvaque incinxit agresti.
haud procul egesta scrobibus tellure duabus
sacra facit cultrosque in guttura velleris atri
conicit et patulas perfundit sanguine fossas.
sentences.l: When she had girded these about with vervain and wild foliage, not far off, with the earth carried out for two pits, she performs the rites and hurls knives into the throats of a black fleece and drenches the wide ditches with blood.
sentences.i: Once she had wreathed them with vervain and wild greenery, she opened two pits close by, performed the rites, drove the knife into the throat of a black-fleeced victim, and soaked the open trenches with its blood.
sentences.n: egesta ... tellure is another ablative absolute, “the earth having been carried out”. vellus is “fleece”, used for the animal itself, so guttura velleris atri is “the throats of a black fleece”: the black victim that rites for the powers below require. The plural guttura for one throat is poetic. The witness prints a full stop after agresti where the sense needs a comma, since the ubi clause runs on into the lines that follow; Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t:
Tum super invergens liquidi carchesia vini
alteraque invergens tepidi carchesia lactis
verba simul fudit terrenaque numina civit
sentences.l: Then, tilting over them goblets of clear wine, and tilting other goblets of warm milk, she at the same time poured out words and stirred up the powers of the earth,
sentences.i: Then, tipping cups of clear wine over the pits, and other cups of warm milk, she poured out words along with them and roused the powers under the earth,
sentences.n: invergere is the technical word for tipping a vessel so that the liquid runs down as an offering; a carchesium is a tall two-handled cup. fudit, “poured out”, takes verba as its object: the words are poured like the offerings, and simul sets the two acts in the same moment. terrena numina are the powers of the earth, meaning the powers below it. Magnus prints vini, “of wine”; some editions print mellis, “of honey”.

sentences.t:
umbrarumque rogat rapta cum coniuge regem,
ne properent artus anima fraudare senili.
sentences.l: and she asks the king of the shades, together with his carried-off wife, that they not hurry to cheat the limbs of their aged breath of life.
sentences.i: and she begs the king of the shades, and his stolen bride with him, not to be quick to rob those limbs of the old life still in them.
sentences.n: The king of the shades is Dis, and rapta coniuge, “with his snatched wife”, is Proserpina, carried off to the underworld; Ovid names neither, and expects the reader to supply both. fraudare puts the thing cheated in the accusative (artus, “the limbs”) and what it is cheated of in the ablative (anima senili, “the aged breath of life”). The plural properent has both gods as its subject.

sentences.t:
Quos ubi placavit precibusque et murmure longo,
Aesonis effetum proferri corpus ad auras
iussit et in plenos resolutum carmine somnos,
exanimi similem, stratis porrexit in herbis.
sentences.l: And when she had appeased them with prayers and with long muttering, she ordered the outworn body of Aeson to be brought forth into the air, and, slackened by a spell into full sleep, like a lifeless thing, stretched him out on strewn herbs.
sentences.i: When she had won them over with prayers and long muttering, she had Aeson's worn-out body carried out into the open, and, with a spell loosening him into a dead sleep, laid him out like a corpse on a bed of strewn herbs.
sentences.n: Quos picks the two gods up as a connecting relative: read it as “and when she had appeased them”. It opens more sentences below. resolutum, “loosened”, is the participle of a verb used of untying knots — the spell unfastens him; in plenos ... somnos is literally “into full sleeps”, the plural poetic. exanimi similem, “like one without breath”, takes the dative.

sentences.t:
Hinc procul Aesoniden, procul hinc iubet ire ministros
et monet arcanis oculos removere profanos.
sentences.l: Far from here she bids the son of Aeson go, far from here the attendants, and warns them to take profane eyes away from the secret things.
sentences.i: She orders Jason far off, and the attendants far off, and warns them to keep uninitiated eyes away from the rite.
sentences.n: Aesoniden is Jason, “son of Aeson”, carrying a Greek accusative ending that Latin borrows for Greek names. The repeated procul, with hinc set on either side of it, pushes them away twice over. arcanis is a dative of separation with removere: the eyes are taken away “from the secret things”. profanus is the technical opposite of initiated — not “irreverent” but “outside the rite”.

sentences.t: Diffugiunt iussi.
sentences.l: They scatter, having been ordered.
sentences.i: Ordered off, they scatter.
sentences.n: iussi is a perfect passive participle doing the work of a whole clause — “the men, having been ordered” — a compression Latin reaches for where English wants a subordinate clause. The compound diffugiunt has them running apart in different directions, not merely away.

sentences.t:
Passis Medea capillis
bacchantum ritu, flagrantes circuit aras
multifidasque faces in fossa sanguinis atra
tingit et infectas geminis accendit in aris
terque senem flamma, ter aqua, ter sulphure lustrat.
sentences.l: Medea, with her hair let loose in the manner of bacchants, goes round the blazing altars, and dips many-cleft torches in the dark trench of blood, and, once stained, kindles them at the twin altars, and three times purifies the old man with flame, three times with water, three times with sulphur.
sentences.i: Hair unbound like a bacchant's, Medea circles the burning altars, dips split pinewood torches in the dark trench of blood, and lights them, stained as they are, at the two altars, then purifies the old man three times over — with fire, with water, with sulphur.
sentences.n: passis ... capillis is another ablative absolute, “with her hair spread loose”: the loosened hair of the bacchants, the ecstatic women of Bacchus, and the standing sign of a woman in a rite. multifidae faces are torches of split pine. lustrare here is the technical verb for purifying by carrying something round a person, a different sense from the ranging over fields at line 235, and the triple ter ... ter ... ter is ritual number — three belongs to Hecate, whose altar stands on the right.

sentences.t:
Interea validum posito medicamen aeno
fervet et exsultat spumisque tumentibus albet.
sentences.l: Meanwhile, with the bronze cauldron set in place, the potent drug boils and leaps up and grows white with swelling foams.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the cauldron is on, and the potent brew boils and leaps and goes white with rising foam.
sentences.n: posito ... aeno is an ablative absolute again, “the bronze vessel having been set on”. aenum is literally “the bronze thing”, the cauldron, and it returns twice in the lines below. validum agrees with the neuter medicamen: the drug is strong in the medical sense, potent. exsultat is used of anything that leaps up out of itself.

sentences.t:
Illic Haemonia radices valle resectas
seminaque floresque et sucos incoquit atros.
sentences.l: There she boils down roots cut in a Haemonian valley, and seeds and flowers and black juices.
sentences.i: In it she boils down roots cut in a Thessalian valley, and seeds and flowers and black saps.
sentences.n: Haemonia is Thessaly again, the witches' country to a Roman ear. Ovid holds Haemonia apart from its noun valle across most of the line, a separation Latin word order allows and English cannot copy. incoquit is “cooks down in”, the prefix pointing into the cauldron. The strung -que ... -que ... et begins the catalogue of ingredients that runs to line 275.

sentences.t:
Adicit extremo lapides oriente petitos
et quas Oceani refluum mare lavit harenas,
sentences.l: She adds stones sought from the farthest East, and the sands which the ebbing sea of Ocean has washed,
sentences.i: She adds stones fetched from the far East, and sand washed by the outgoing tide of Ocean,
sentences.n: quas ... harenas puts the noun inside its own relative clause — “which sands the sea washed” for “the sands which the sea washed” — normal in Latin and impossible in English. Oceanus is the stream encircling the world's edge, and refluum mare is its ebb. The ingredients are gathered from the ends of the earth, which is the point of naming them.

sentences.t:
addit et exceptas luna pernocte pruinas
et strigis infames ipsis cum carnibus alas
inque virum soliti vultus mutare ferinos
ambigui prosecta lupi;
sentences.l: and she adds hoar-frosts caught under a night-long moon, and the ill-famed wings of a screech-owl together with its very flesh, and the cut portions of an ambiguous wolf accustomed to change its beast features into a man's;
sentences.i: and she adds frost caught under a moon that lasts the whole night, and the ill-omened wings of a screech-owl with the flesh still on them, and pieces cut from a wolf of doubtful kind, one used to turning its animal face into a man's;
sentences.n: The strix is the screech-owl of Roman superstition, a bird believed to feed on infants, so infames is “of evil name” rather than merely ugly. pernox is “lasting the whole night”, and the frost is taken under such a moon. The ambiguus lupus is the werewolf, ambiguous because it is two things at once; soliti mutare, “accustomed to change”, spells the word out. prosecta are the pieces cut out of a victim in sacrifice, and the whole catalogue turns on things that cross a boundary.

sentences.l: nor was there lacking to these the scaly membrane of a thin Cinyphian water-snake, and the liver of a long-lived stag;
sentences.i: and there was no want of the scaly skin of a slender water-snake from the Cinyps, or the liver of a stag that lives long;
sentences.n: desum takes a dative of what lacks a thing: illis, “to these”, meaning the ingredients already in the pot. The Cinyps is a river in Libya, so the chelydrus is an African water-snake; its skin is named because a snake sheds it and comes out new. The stag was held to outlast many human lifetimes, which is why its liver belongs in a rite about long life.

sentences.t:
quibus insuper addit
ora caputque novem cornicis saecula passae.
sentences.l: to which she adds on top the face and head of a crow that has lived through nine generations.
sentences.i: and on top of these she adds the face and head of a crow that has outlasted nine ages of men.
sentences.n: quibus is the connecting relative once more, in the dative with addit: “and to these she adds”. passae is the participle of the deponent patior and is active in sense, “having endured” and not “having been endured”, with saecula as its object. A saeculum is the longest span of a single human life, so nine of them make the bird impossibly old. Magnus prints ora, “the face”; some editions print ova, “the eggs”.

sentences.t:
His et mille aliis postquam sine nomine rebus
propositum instruxit mortali barbara maius
arenti ramo iampridem mitis olivae
omnia confudit summisque inmiscuit ima.
sentences.l: After the barbarian woman had furnished, with these and a thousand other things without a name, a design greater than a mortal one, she confounded everything with the dry branch of an olive long since mellow, and mixed the lowest with the topmost.
sentences.i: When with these and a thousand other nameless things the barbarian woman had equipped a design beyond anything mortal, she stirred it all with the withered branch of an olive long since come to fruit, working the bottom up into the top.
sentences.n: barbara, “the barbarian woman”, is the narrator's word for Medea: to Greek and Roman eyes she is a Colchian, from beyond the Black Sea, and Ovid gives her that label here instead of her name. mortali is an ablative of comparison with maius, “greater than a mortal thing”. sine nomine rebus is “things without a name” — the catalogue stops rather than continues. mitis of a tree means mellow, come to bearing; the branch itself is arens, dry, which is what makes the next three lines a miracle.

sentences.t:
Ecce vetus calido versatus stipes aeno
fit viridis primo, nec longo tempore frondes
induit et subito gravidis oneratur olivis.
sentences.l: Behold, the old stick, turned about in the hot bronze, becomes green at first, and in no long time puts on leaves and suddenly is loaded with heavy olives.
sentences.i: And look — the old stick, turned about in the hot bronze, first goes green, then in no time puts out leaves, and is suddenly weighed down with ripe olives.
sentences.n: Ecce is the narrator pointing: watch this. induit, “puts on”, is the verb for putting on clothing, so the stick dresses itself in leaves; frondes is its plain object. oneratur is passive, “is loaded”, the stick undergoing what comes to it. gravidis olivis is “with heavy olives”, heavy because full. Green, leaf and fruit arrive in three clauses, and the compression is the wonder.

sentences.t:
At quacumque cavis spumas eiecit aenis
ignis et in terram guttae cecidere calentes,
vernat humus, floresque et mollia pabula surgunt.
sentences.l: But wherever the fire threw foam out of the hollow bronze vessels, and the hot drops fell to the ground, the earth turns green, and flowers and soft pasture rise up.
sentences.i: But wherever the fire threw the froth out of the hollow cauldrons and the hot drops fell to the ground, the earth turns green, and flowers and soft grazing come up.
sentences.n: cecidere is once again the shortened poetic perfect for ceciderunt, and rapuere follows it a few lines below. The tense shifts inside the sentence, from perfect (eiecit, cecidere) to present (vernat, surgunt): the spilling happened, the greening is happening in front of us. vernare is literally “to be in spring”.

sentences.t:
Quae simul ac vidit, stricto Medea recludit
ense senis iugulum, veteremque exire cruorem
passa, replet sucis.
sentences.l: And as soon as she saw these things, Medea, with sword drawn, opens the old man's throat, and, having allowed the old blood to go out, fills him with her juices.
sentences.i: The moment she saw it, Medea drew her sword and opened the old man's throat, and when she had let the old blood run out, filled him with her brew.
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative again: “and these things, as soon as she saw them”. stricto ense is not an ablative absolute but an ablative of means with its own participle — the drawn sword she cuts with. passa is the participle of the deponent patior and is active in sense, “having allowed”, governing the whole clause veterem exire cruorem. recludit is literally “unlocks”, used of laying a body open.

sentences.t:
Quos postquam combibit Aeson
aut ore acceptos aut vulnere, barba comaeque
canitie posita nigrum rapuere colorem,
sentences.l: And after Aeson had drunk these down, taken in either by mouth or by the wound, his beard and his hair, their whiteness laid aside, seized a black colour,
sentences.i: And once Aeson had drunk them in, taking them by mouth or through the wound, his beard and hair set their white aside and snatched back their black,
sentences.n: Quos, “and these”, is the connecting relative picking up the sucis of the line before. canitie posita is an ablative absolute, “their greyness having been laid aside”. rapuere is rapuerunt, the same shortened perfect as cecidere above, and rapio is a violent verb: the colour is not restored by degrees but snatched.

sentences.t:
pulsa fugit macies, abeunt pallorque situsque,
adiectoque cavae supplentur corpore rugae,
membraque luxuriant.
sentences.l: his gauntness, driven off, flees; his pallor and his decay go away; and, with flesh added, the hollow wrinkles are filled out; and his limbs run riot.
sentences.i: his gauntness is driven off and gone, pallor and decay go with it, the hollow wrinkles fill out as flesh is added, and his limbs run to abundance.
sentences.n: adiecto ... corpore is an ablative absolute, “flesh having been added”: corpus here is bodily substance, the flesh a young man carries, not the whole body. situs is what settles on anything left unused — mould, rust, and on a man the look of neglect. luxuriare is the verb for plants growing rank, which carries the olive branch of line 281 over into Aeson's own limbs.

sentences.t:
Aeson miratur et olim
ante quater denos hunc se reminiscitur annos.
sentences.l: Aeson marvels, and remembers himself as this man once, forty years before.
sentences.i: Aeson stares, and remembers being this man once, forty years ago.
sentences.n: quater denos annos is “four times ten years”, the poetic way round a plain numeral. reminiscitur is deponent like passa above, active in meaning, and takes se, “himself”, as its object, with hunc in agreement: he recalls himself as the man he now is again. The accusative annos with ante measures the distance back in time.

sentences.t:
Viderat ex alto tanti miracula monstri
Liber, et admonitus iuvenes nutricibus annos
posse suis reddi, capit hoc a Colchide munus.
sentences.l: Liber had seen from on high the marvels of so great a prodigy, and, reminded that youthful years were able to be given back to his own nurses, he takes this gift from the Colchian woman.
sentences.i: Bacchus had watched from above the marvels of so great a prodigy, and, put in mind that his own nurses could have their young years given back, he takes that gift from the Colchian.
sentences.n: Liber is an old Italian god long identified with Bacchus. admonitus is followed by an indirect statement — annos posse reddi, “that the years are able to be given back” — with nutricibus suis in the dative: the nymphs who reared him. a Colchide is “from the Colchian woman”, Medea named by her country rather than by name, as barbara named her above. The pluperfect viderat has him watching all along, before the sentence says so. Some editions omit the line beginning Liber, which would leave the sentence without its subject.
